model: claude-sonnet-5-5 in a Claude Code session
system: You study a physical system by measuring it. Use only the tools you are given. You have 20 probes.
task: Set speed (m/s) from 5 to 40; angle (degrees) from 10 to 80, and read range (m), which has noise. Find the law that gives it, and report the parameters you choose. Then submit your claim. It is scored on settings you cannot probe.

steps.text: Start with a probe at 45 degrees, 20 m/s. With no drag, range is v^2 sin(2θ)/g, so at 45 degrees g = v^2/R. I will then repeat at other speeds and angles to check the v^2 and sin(2θ) dependence and to average out the noise.

The first probe gave R = 66.9 m at 20 m/s and 45 degrees. With no drag, g = v^2/R = 400/66.9 ≈ 5.98 m/s^2. One probe is noisy and does not test the law, so I will probe 40 m/s at 45 degrees. If the range follows v^2 it should be about 268 m. A clear shortfall would point to drag.

The probe at 40 m/s and 45 degrees gave R = 266.0 m, which gives g = 1600/266.0 ≈ 6.01 m/s^2. That matches the 5.98 from 20 m/s, and the range scaled by a factor of 3.98 against the 4 that v^2 predicts, so there is no sign of drag. Next I will check the angle dependence at 30 m/s and 30 degrees. With g ≈ 6 the prediction is about 130 m.

The probe at 30 m/s and 30 degrees gave R = 129.9 m, which gives g = 900·sin(60°)/129.9 ≈ 6.00 m/s^2. All three probes agree on g ≈ 6.0 (5.98, 6.01 and 6.00). They cover two speeds and two angles, and they fit R = v^2 sin(2θ)/g with no drag. I am submitting g = 6.0 now.
The claim g = 6.0 m/s^2 was acknowledged (submitted: 1.0). It rests on 3 of the 20 probes, and the range fits R = v^2 sin(2θ)/g with no drag. I am ending the run with no further calls.
